title: Does Verifier Feedback Reduce Residual Unsafe Vendor CLI Configurations? A Paired Controlled Fault‑Injection Study
abstract: We report a preregistered controlled‑challenge paired experiment that measured whether exposing deterministic verifier diagnostics to an LLM repair workflow reduces residual unsafe or invalid vendor‑CLI configurations compared with blind repair. Under the preregistered adapter hosted_netops_validator_feedback_repair_v2 with shared_controlled_fault_candidate semantics we planned 40 paired tasks and observed 39 complete pairs (one source generation invalid and excluded per preregistered rules). Baseline (blind repair) satisfied the deterministic verifier+simulator acceptance predicate in 30/39 pairs (76.92%); guarded (verifier‑guided) satisfied it in 38/39 pairs (97.44%). Paired contingency: n11=29, n10=9 (guarded‑only), n01=1 (baseline‑only), n00=0. The paired absolute difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.20512820512820507 (20.51 percentage points); two‑sided exact paired test p = 0.021484375; 95% paired‑bootstrap percentile CI = [0.07692307692307693, 0.358974358974359] (bootstrap resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). Confirmatory execution used the declared model gpt‑5‑mini and consumed 118 hosted‑model calls (<=120). The preregistered confirmatory harmful‑overrepair aggregation was not computed in the archived confirmatory summary and therefore remains unresolved for confirmatory inference; the frozen harmful‑change mapping and per‑episode validator traces were recorded and enable deterministic independent recomputation. We present the preregistered primary result, expand design rationale, interpret the discordant‑pair structure and observed failure modes grounded in execution traces, and state limitations and reproducibility guidance without altering the preregistered scientific record.

sections.introduction: Large language models (LLMs) are being integrated into network operations (NetOps) workflows for tasks from intent translation to automated remediation. A standard safety architecture is generate–verify–repair (GVR): generated candidates are passed through deterministic verifiers and failing candidates produce diagnostics that a generator/repair model can use to attempt fixes. Prior evaluations in code and IaC contexts document that deterministic verifiers raise verifier‑detected pass rates but can expose new failure modes (e.g., verifier‑exploitation) and incur interaction costs [F1–F4]. Controlled, paired evidence specific to vendor CLI templates with deterministic, preregistered fault operators is limited (gap articulated in preregistration). We designed a paired, controlled‑challenge experiment to isolate the effect of exposing verifier diagnostics to an LLM repair model when the same deterministically injected fault candidate is shared across arms. Our primary research question: when an LLM repair model encounters a deterministically injected, actionable vendor‑CLI fault, does deterministic verifier feedback reduce the residual rate of unsafe or invalid configurations compared with blind repair under matched repair budgets?
sections.related_work: The literature establishes several relevant, but domain‑limited, findings. First, GVR pipelines that interpose deterministic verifiers between stochastic generation and acceptance reliably detect mechanically verifiable defects and improve verifier pass rates on evaluated code/IaC/DSL tasks; these are pipeline evaluations and case studies rather than broad NetOps replications [doi:10.2139/ssrn.6754899; W7171267824]. Second, verifier‑guided iterative refinement raises pass@1 / validator pass rates in IaC benchmarks while reducing specific verifier‑detected failure classes in those domains; the magnitude and generality depend on verifier design and repair budget. Third, enforcing runtime verification imposes a measurable interaction and compute overhead (a “verifier tax”) that depends on horizon and design choices [W7140238430]. Fourth, single‑proxy verifiers in iterative loops can be exploited: optimization toward the verifier proxy can degrade the underlying target property (verifier‑exploitation) in some controlled studies [doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10187492/v1]. Finally, surveys and field case studies of LLM assistance in NetOps/AIOps emphasize that read‑oriented benefits do not directly imply safe closed‑loop changes without careful verification and conservative orchestration [W7161165783; W7162044117]. These prior findings motivate our controlled pairing: deterministic controlled faults guarantee intervention activation, and shared candidate semantics isolate the feedback‑exposure effect while keeping repair budgets matched.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The study was preregistered under vCLI_fault_injection_repair_2026_A_prereg_v1. The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline: the per‑task difference in binary success where success requires both the deterministic vendor‑CLI validator and the simulator‑based compliance check to accept the final candidate.

Adapter and pairing semantics. Confirmatory execution used the hosted_netops_validator_feedback_repair_v2 adapter under shared_controlled_fault_candidate semantics. Under those semantics exactly one deterministically injected controlled‑fault candidate was produced per task index and reused unchanged across both experimental conditions; exactly one sampled initial generation per task pair was produced and shared by both arms. Baseline denotes blind repair (the repair model did not receive validator diagnostics); guarded denotes the same repair model receiving the deterministic validator diagnostics. Because the shared candidate and matched repair budget are preserved across arms, observed differences isolate the effect of exposing diagnostics under the adapter contract.

Model sampling and runtime parameters. The declared model was gpt‑5‑mini. The archived model configuration records temperature = null (unset); null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. The adapter contract produced exactly one sampled initial generation per pair which was reused by both arms; this design does not measure effects of independent first‑pass sampling across conditions.

Controlled fault bank and scoring. The confirmatory run used 40 preregistered deterministic controlled faults injected into vendor‑CLI template tasks (task indices 1..40). The primary success predicate required agreement between a deterministic vendor‑CLI validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and a simulator‑based compliance check. A frozen harmful‑change mapping (an episode is harmful if post‑repair validation contains PROTECTED_INTERFACE_CHANGE or UNINTENDED_STATE_CHANGE) was recorded before execution. All per‑episode validator traces and the frozen mapping were recorded during execution and are sufficient to deterministically reaggregate the preregistered harmful‑overrepair statistic; because the archived confirmatory summary did not compute that aggregation, it remains unresolved for confirmatory inference here.

Execution accounting and analysis plan. Planned confirmatory pairs = 40; the adapter produced 78 completed episodes (two failed adapter episodes), yielding 39 complete pairs after the preregistered 'complete_pair_primary' exclusion rule (one source generation invalid). Hosted‑model calls used = 118 (<= planned maximum 120). Primary analysis executed the preregistered exact two‑sided paired binary test (exact McNemar equivalent) and a paired‑bootstrap (percentile) CI (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). Discordant counts, absolute paired difference, p‑value, and CI are reported. Sensitivity options (treating missing episodes as failures) were preregistered but the primary result uses complete_pair_primary.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and primary outcome. Planned pairs = 40; completed pairs analyzed = 39 (one pair excluded because its source generation was invalid/unscorable per the preregistered rule). Hosted model calls used = 118 (<=120). Source generation attempts = 40 (source_valid_count = 39; source_invalid_or_failed_count = 1).

Primary confirmatory result (complete_pairs = 39). Baseline (blind repair) success = 30/39 = 0.7692307692307693. Guarded (verifier‑guided) success = 38/39 = 0.9743589743589743. Paired contingency counts (guarded, baseline): n11 = 29, n10 = 9 (guarded‑only successes), n01 = 1 (baseline‑only success), n00 = 0. Paired estimate (guarded − baseline) = 0.20512820512820507 (20.51 percentage points). Exact two‑sided paired test p = 0.021484375. 95% paired‑bootstrap percentile CI = [0.07692307692307693, 0.358974358974359] (bootstrap_resamples = 10000, bootstrap_seed = 1729).

Discordant‑pair structure and interpretation. The preponderance of n10 (9 guarded‑only successes versus 1 baseline‑only) drives the observed positive paired difference. Under McNemar‑type logic the observed asymmetry in discordants supports an effect attributable to diagnostics exposure given the shared initial candidate and matched repair budgets. The paired bootstrap CI excludes zero and indicates the effect is not negligible at the sample size realized, but the CI width (approx. 28 percentage‑points) reflects finite sample uncertainty given complete_pairs = 39.

Representative failure‑mode evidence from per‑episode traces. Per‑episode validator traces recorded during execution show repeated violation codes that explain why guarded repairs typically succeeded where baseline sometimes failed. Examples in the archived scoring artifacts include the violation codes PROTECTED_INTERFACE_CHANGE, UNINTENDED_STATE_CHANGE, and FINAL_STATE_MISMATCH (see execution/scoring examples for tasks 000001–000003). In several guarded episodes the validator diagnostics explicitly identified protected fields or mismatched final state; the repair model exposed to these diagnostics produced targeted edits that avoided protected‑interface modifications or restored required command sequences (e.g., source/validation/validation_after fields in task‑000001 and task‑000003 artifacts). Conversely, baseline repairs that succeeded sometimes did so by preserving the initially shared source candidate or by applying corrective edits blind to the validator's explicit violation codes; the recorded single baseline‑only success (n01 = 1) indicates such cases are uncommon under these controlled faults.

Missingness and unresolved preregistered safety aggregation. One pair was excluded because its source generation was invalid and unscorable per preregistration (complete_pair_primary). The preregistered harmful‑overrepair aggregation (safety hypothesis bounding harmful over‑repair) was not computed in the archived confirmatory summary and therefore remains unresolved for confirmatory inference. The frozen harmful‑change labeling mapping and per‑episode validator traces required to compute that aggregation were recorded and permit deterministic reaggregation by independent auditors; any harmful‑overrepair numbers computed outside the archived confirmatory summary are exploratory.
sections.discussion:
Why the paired shared‑candidate design is appropriate. The shared_controlled_fault_candidate semantics were chosen to isolate the causal effect of exposing deterministic diagnostics while holding the initial injected fault candidate and generation budget constant across arms. Because both arms received the same initial candidate and each arm received its permitted repair opportunity, differences in final acceptance rates can be attributed to diagnostics exposure rather than to differences in first‑pass generations, injected faults, or repair budget. This design answers a practically relevant estimand: given a single faulty candidate and a matched repair budget, does exposing deterministic verifier diagnostics increase the probability that an LLM repair produces a verifier+simulator‑acceptable configuration?

Mechanistic interpretation of observed improvements. The archived validator traces show diagnostics that pinpoint protected fields (PROTECTED_INTERFACE_CHANGE), unintended edits (UNINTENDED_STATE_CHANGE), or final‑state mismatches (FINAL_STATE_MISMATCH). Guarded repairs commonly include edits that directly address the flagged violation codes (for example, re‑inserting a required restore command or omitting a protected‑interface modification), consistent with the hypothesis that explicit diagnostics can focus a repair model's constrained generation and thereby reduce residual invalid outcomes. The prevalence of n10 relative to n01 indicates guarded repairs more often remedied verifier‑detectable defects that blind repair left unresolved.

Uncertainty, power, and planned versus observed effect. The preregistered power plan targeted a detectable absolute paired difference near ~30 percentage points with n = 40. The observed absolute difference (≈20.51 percentage points) is smaller than the design target but statistically detectable here: exact paired p = 0.0215 and the paired‑bootstrap 95% CI excludes zero. The CI magnitude shows finite‑sample uncertainty; the study does not claim the observed point estimate is the population effect but does provide a preregistered, verifiable paired estimate and CI. With only 39 complete pairs, subgroup or per‑fault‑class comparisons lack confirmatory power and must be treated as exploratory.

Failure modes, verifier‑exploitation risk, and mitigations. The study used a short, matched repair budget and single repair opportunity, which reduces iterative amplification risks but does not eliminate verifier‑exploitation in longer‑horizon agentic pipelines. Execution traces show no systematic evidence of diagnostics being misused to introduce new, undetected violations in this short‑horizon setting, but the preregistered harmful‑overrepair aggregation was not computed in the archived confirmatory summary and hence the safety verdict is unresolved for confirmatory inference. Practical mitigations suggested by both the literature and our design include multi‑verifier ensembles, explicit harmful‑change constraints (the frozen harmful‑change mapping used here is an example), calibrated abstention thresholds, and uncertainty quantification integrated into repair decisions.

Operational implications and verifier tax. Guarded repairs improved verifier+simulator acceptance on this controlled fault bank, but verifier‑guided workflows incur additional interaction and compute overhead: confirmatory execution consumed 118 hosted‑model calls under the matched budget. These counts permit exploratory cost‑per‑avoided‑failure calculations but do not suffice to establish operational feasibility at NetOps scale. Large‑scale deployment tradeoffs (latency, operator triage workload, cost per operation) remain an open empirical question (see unresolved questions in the preregistration and evidence synthesis).

Threats to validity and generalization. Internal validity: shared‑candidate pairing and matching of repair budgets isolate diagnostics exposure, but model sampling nondeterminism (temperature = null/unset) and the single initial sampled generation per pair limit claims about first‑pass generation effects. Construct validity: primary success required agreement between a deterministic validator and a simulator; simulator fidelity and validator coverage bound the operational meaning of “valid.” External validity: confirmatory execution used one declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) and a synthetic, template‑based controlled fault bank; generalization to diverse vendor equipment, live operator streams, or other models is limited. Conclusion validity: 39 complete pairs support detection of the observed magnitude but limit precision for subgroup inference; exploratory per‑fault‑class or per‑difficulty analyses are hypothesis‑generating only.
sections.conclusion: In this preregistered controlled‑challenge paired experiment using a hosted validator‑feedback repair adapter with shared controlled‑fault candidates, exposing deterministic verifier diagnostics to an LLM repair workflow produced a statistically detectable and substantial increase in verifier+simulator‑validated configuration success (approx. +20.51 percentage points; p = 0.021484375; 95% CI [0.07692307692307693, 0.358974358974359]). This result is bounded to the preregistered synthetic task bank, the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini), the adapter pairing semantics, and the deterministic verifier and simulator used in execution. The preregistered confirmatory harmful‑overrepair test was not present in the archived confirmatory summary and therefore remains unresolved for confirmatory inference; the frozen harmful‑change mapping and recorded per‑episode validator traces provide exact inputs for independent deterministic reconstruction of that preregistered safety statistic. We recommend multi‑model, multi‑verifier replications, full confirmatory computation of preregistered safety aggregations, and larger‑scale cost/latency studies to assess operational feasibility and safety in production NetOps settings.

disclosure_statement: Preregistration: vCLI_fault_injection_repair_2026_A_prereg_v1. Adapter family used for confirmatory execution: hosted_netops_validator_feedback_repair_v2. Declared model used for confirmatory execution: gpt‑5‑mini. Exact initial master prompt archived as provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: f781dd7978328198146d586cf33e0f4b783c8db126bd0f16fcd13699455ebb10). Human role and autonomy boundary: a Research Director selected the topic family and pre‑lock constraints; after the autonomy lock the autonomous system performed literature verification, preregistration, experiment execution, analysis, and manuscript generation; no manual human editing of technical manuscript content occurred after the lock. Execution semantics: the archived model configuration records temperature = null (unset); null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. Pairing semantics: exactly one sampled initial generation per task pair was performed and reused by both arms under shared_controlled_fault_candidate semantics; baseline denotes blind repair (no validator diagnostics exposed) and guarded denotes repair with deterministic validator diagnostics exposed. The preregistered harmful‑change labeling mapping used to define the planned safety aggregation was frozen before execution; the mapping and per‑episode validation traces required to compute the preregistered harmful‑overrepair aggregation were recorded during execution. All per‑episode traces, scored artifacts, and transformation mappings needed to reproduce the preregistered secondary aggregations were recorded in the archived evidence bundle. The study followed the preregistered stopping rule.
limitations: Synthetic controlled‑fault task bank: tasks were deterministically injected and do not represent a broad naturalistic distribution of production NetOps incidents; external validity to live operator workloads is limited.
Single‑model and single‑adapter evaluation: confirmatory execution used only the declared model gpt‑5‑mini and one adapter family; results do not establish multi‑model generality.
Simulator‑backed primary success predicate: primary success required agreement of deterministic verifier and simulator; simulator fidelity and validator coverage constrain construct validity.

Sample size and power: complete_pairs = 39 provides detectable effects of the observed magnitude but limits precision for subgroup and per‑fault‑class inference; exploratory subgroup analyses are not confirmatory.
Operational cost/latency unresolved for deployment: execution was instrumented and counts were recorded, but large‑scale operational feasibility (verifier tax tradeoffs) requires larger‑scale study.

Verifier‑exploitation and long‑horizon agentic pathologies remain possible: this controlled setting mitigates some risks, but broader agentic workflows need additional defenses (multi‑verifier designs, calibrated abstention, uncertainty quantification).

Preregistered confirmatory harmful‑overrepair test not present in archived confirmatory summary: the archived confirmatory analysis executor did not compute the preregistered harmful‑overrepair aggregation; the per‑episode traces and the frozen mapping required to compute it were recorded and are available for independent reaggregation, but the preregistered confirmatory safety verdict is therefore unresolved in this paper.
